title: What the compiler makes of a switch

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, how does the order of the `case` labels change the speed of an `int` switch?

options.text: It changes it a lot, as the JVM tries each case from the top down
options.says: The page says javac compiles the switch to a direct jump or a binary search, whatever the order.

options.text: It changes it a little, as the JIT moves the first case to the front
options.says: The page says case order does not affect performance at all.

options.text: It changes nothing, as javac emits a jump table or a sorted lookup
options.says: The page says javac compiles an int switch to a tableswitch or a lookupswitch, whatever the order in the source.

questions.stem: What does this page require of the values written after `case`?

options.text: Values fixed at compile time, each one distinct from the rest
options.says: The page says case labels must be compile-time constants, and each case value must be unique.

options.text: Values of the selector's type, worked out as each case is reached
options.says: The page says case labels must be compile-time constants, not values worked out at run time.

options.text: Values written as literals, since named constants are refused
options.says: The page asks for compile-time constants, which named constants can be; it does not limit labels to literals.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: Case order does not affect speed: javac compiles an int switch to a tableswitch or a lookupswitch.
Case labels must be unique compile-time constants.
